sources.entry: Back to Basics, Joel Spolsky. Explains why learning low level programming is important.

summary.title: Back to Basics
summary.one_liner: Low-level fundamentals (C strings, malloc, and byte-level data layout) explain many high-level performance and architecture problems, such as quadratic string concatenation and why XML is slow to query.
takeaways: C strings are null-terminated, so finding their length is a linear scan, and they cannot hold zero bytes.
Repeated strcat rescans the destination each time, giving n-squared 'Shlemiel the painter' behaviour; returning a pointer to the end of the string makes it linear.
Pascal length-prefixed strings give constant-time length lookup and can hold zeros, but are limited to 255 bytes.
Fixed-size records let a relational database step to the next row with one pointer addition, while XML requires parsing and scanning, which is much slower.
Understanding bytes, malloc and memory layout helps make better high-level architecture decisions.
summary.summary: Joel Spolsky argues that programmers should understand the lowest levels (CPU, bytes, C strings, malloc) because these details drive high-level performance and architecture decisions. He walks through C strcat, showing why repeated concatenation is quadratic and how returning an end pointer fixes it, then compares null-terminated and Pascal strings. He discusses malloc's free chain, power-of-two and doubling allocation strategies, and buffer overflows. The essay closes by contrasting fixed-offset relational records with XML parsing, and by arguing that CS education should start from C and the CPU.
